theory.title: Hops: One Router at a Time
theory.plainObjective: Navigate through two routers in a chain - each one makes its own independent decision about where to send you.
theory.summary: Every message you send online crosses many routers like this. Each one reads only the destination address and forwards the packet without knowing the full path ahead.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Each router decides independently
bodyParagraphs.text: Each router you pass through counts as one hop. At every hop, that router reads your destination IP and consults its own routing table - completely independent of every other router on the path. Routers do not coordinate with each other; each one makes a local decision based only on what it knows.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Time to Live (TTL)
bodyParagraphs.text: A TTL counter is embedded in every packet. Each router decrements it by 1 before forwarding. If TTL reaches 0, the packet is dropped. This prevents packets from circling the internet indefinitely when routing loops occur.

theory.mission:
You are 10.0.1.5 delivering to 10.0.2.10.

Two routers stand between you and the destination. At each hop, read that router's table independently and follow the matching exit.

termIntroductions.headline: TTL - Time to Live
termIntroductions.body: Every packet carries a TTL counter. Each router decrements it by 1. If TTL hits 0, the packet is dropped. This stops packets from looping the internet forever.

termIntroductions.headline: Hop
termIntroductions.body: Each router a packet passes through is one hop. You just made your first hop from R1 to R2. Real internet traffic crosses dozens of hops to reach its destination.
